title: Postman for MCP
spec: CC9 · debugging a server with the Inspector
intro: When a tool misbehaves in Claude Code you have two suspects: your server returned the wrong thing, or Claude sent the wrong arguments. The Inspector settles it in one screen, because it speaks the same JSON-RPC Claude Code does.

provenance.source: a narrated session against the CC9 lab's ucc_lookup FastMCP server; commands, tool names and the JSON-RPC frames are taken from the module, terminal timing and ids are reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: CC9 Lab 2 — npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py.

steps.title: Boot the Inspector against your server
narrative: One command. The Inspector spawns server.py as a subprocess over stdio, sits between you and it as a proxy, and opens a browser UI with the auth token already in the URL.

Two ports, and knowing which is which saves you ten minutes later: 6277 is the proxy that actually holds the stdio pipe to your server, 6274 is the UI you look at. If the UI loads but nothing connects, the problem is at 6277 — your subprocess died on startup.
steps.youDo: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py, then open the pre-filled URL, pick stdio transport and click Connect.

the token in the URL, and that 6277 is free

view.note: stdio transport is stdout. Anything you print that is not a JSON-RPC frame corrupts the stream — which is why logging goes through ctx.info, not print.

steps.title: Read the schema Claude reads
narrative: Click Tools. The Inspector issues tools/list and renders a form for each tool derived from your Python type hints — lookup_filing(po_number: str) becomes one text field.

This is the same payload Claude Code receives when it decides whether to call your tool. Which makes the Tools tab a description review, not just a debugging screen: if the docstring is vague here, the model will pick the wrong tool there. ucc_lookup's docstring earns its keep by saying when to call — "whenever a user mentions a PO# or asks about filing status" — and what shape comes back.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing yet — Claude is not in this loop. That is the point: you are testing the server in isolation before any model gets a vote.

terminal.text:
lookup_filing   Look up a UCC filing by purchase order number.
search_debtor   Search filings by debtor name (case-insensitive substring).

before.title: THE SCHEMA — form fields on the left, model affordance on the right

data.name: lookup_filing
data.description: Look up a UCC filing by purchase order number. Use whenever a user mentions a PO# or asks about filing status. Returns: {po_number, debtor, status, filed_at, lien_count}.

view.note: The description is the only thing standing between a correct tool choice and a wrong one. The Inspector is where you notice it is thin.

steps.title: Invoke it and watch the wire
narrative: Fill po_number with PO-100001 and hit Run Tool. Two things appear: the Tool Result panel with your function's return, and the JSON-RPC history pane at the bottom with the raw exchange.

Toggle Before / After to see the pair as one beat — request out, response back, same id. That id is the whole correlation mechanism; when a call appears to hang, look for a request whose id never came back.
Note isError: false sitting next to content. A tool that ran and found nothing is still a successful call at the protocol level — which is the distinction the next step turns on.
steps.youDo: In the Tools tab, click lookup_filing, enter PO-100001, click Run Tool, then expand the request in the history pane.

terminal.text: 12:42:18  ← RECV  id 7  isError: false  ·  1 content block

before.title: → SEND — what Claude Code would send, byte for byte

after.title: ← RECV — what your server sent back

view.note: Your dict came back serialised into a text content block. The model sees that string, not a Python object — so keys and formatting are part of your interface whether you meant them to be or not.

steps.title: Now break it on purpose
narrative: Run the same tool with po_number = NOPE. What comes back tells you which of two very different things your server does when it cannot find something — and Claude treats them completely differently.

A tool-level error keeps the JSON-RPC envelope healthy and puts the problem in content with isError: true. Claude reads that as "the tool ran and told me something", and can retry, ask you, or move on. A protocol-level error — what you get from a bare raise — comes back as error: {code: -32603}, and Claude treats it as the tool being broken. No graceful recovery.

So the rule is small and worth a lot: expected failures (not found, bad argument, rate limited) return a structured dict; only genuine bugs are allowed to raise. Test both shapes here, before a model is anywhere near them.
steps.youDo: Invoke lookup_filing with po_number = NOPE and read the response envelope, not the message.

terminal.text: protocol-level error — Claude would treat this server as broken, not the lookup as empty

cells: "tool ran and returned an error" — can react, retry, or ask
"tool is broken" — treated as fatal, no recovery

view.note: In FastMCP: return a dict with an error key → tool-level. raise Exception(...) → protocol-level.

view.text: A green Inspector does not mean Claude will use your server well — it means the wire works. The two things the Inspector can settle are the two that waste the most time: whether your server returned bad shape, and whether the arguments that arrived were the ones you expected. Everything after that is a description problem, and you fix it in the Tools tab.
